comments.text: this looks to me like 2 different usages- って as a contraction of と or という, and って as a contraction of でも, both of which are more informal then their counterparts.
comments.html: this looks to me like 2 different usages- って as a contraction of と or という, and って as a contraction of でも, both of which are more informal then their counterparts.

comments.text: I never heard of って as a contraction of でも.
comments.html: I never heard of って as a contraction of でも.

comments.text: For example, なんでも can become なんだって and やっても can become やったって in everyday speech without changing the meaning. The best way I could think of to say it was to call it でも.
comments.html: For example, なんでも can become なんだって and やっても can become やったって in everyday speech without changing the meaning. The best way I could think of to say it was to call it でも.

comments.text: I understood this one, but what does it mean when someone says "。。ってのは(rest of the sentence)"？
comments.html: I understood this one, but what does it mean when someone says "。。ってのは(rest of the sentence)"？

comments.text:
@ami I'll have to use Romaji because my computer won't switch to Japanese for some reason right now.

~ tte no wa

is functionally equivalent to

~ to iu no wa

in that it means "~ is defined as", basically. For example:

"Taberu" tte no wa tabemono wo kuti ni ireru koto de aru.

"Eating" means "putting food into your mouth."

I personally find it more pleasing to say "~tte wa" without the "no", or just "~tte".

comments.text:
@nnskage 



i think you mean the ~te form of verbs, not the contraction って

@nnskage 

yes friend there is a rule for the usage of って and て .

てis used when the following verb is used with ん  sound.

For ex-あれはなんてよむんですか.

And, って   is used when the following verb does not consist of the ん  sound.

For ex-あそこ で みどりぐちって かいて あります ね.
